Subodh Ranjan Dutta with Hemayetuddin Ahmed, Advocates.  ------- For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Quayum with Abdul Malek Munshi and Abdul Karim, Advocates ------- For the Opposite Party Nos. 1-3.
parties:
Abdul Ghani Khan ----------- Petitioner.
Vs. 
Abdul Rashid Khan & ors. ----------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted the suit against the opposite parties as defendants for ejectment, realisation of arrear rent and for compensation in the said Court of the learned Small Cause Court Judge stating, inter alia, that the defendants were monthly tenants in the suit premises under the Sonaullah Waqf Estate of which the plaintiff is the Mutwalli at a monthly rent Tk. 125/- which was subsequently enhanced to Tk. 150/- per month since 1st of Baisakh,1390 B.S. The rent was payable according to Bengali month within the expiry of the month for which it was due as per an oral agreement. The defendants did not pay rent regularly. They paid rent for 2/3 months at a time in spite of demand by the landlord. The rent since Baisakh, 1391 B.S. was in arrear. The defendants were habitual defaulters. The plaintiff terminated the tenancy on the expiry of the last day of Sravan, 1391 B.S. by issuing notices on the defendants under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 15th Ashar, 1391 B.S. The defendants received the notices and replied through their Advocate Mr. M.A. Karim on 7.7.84 stating that the contents of the notices were not true. The defendants are trespassers since 1st of Bhadra, 1391 B.S. and for their illegal Occupation of the suit premises since then the plaintiff was entitled to get compensation from them at a rate of Tk. 20/- per day. The plaintiff claims arrear rent from Baisakh to Sravan, 1391 B.S. and also compensation and prayed for khas possession after evicting the defendants from the suit premises. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. They also filed two additional written statements. Their case, inter alia, is that there was oral agreement with the former. Mutwalli Mvi. Rahmatullah to pay the annual rent by instalment and there was no agreement with him for payment of rent within the month for which the rent was due. The defendants offered rent to the plaintiff for the month of Baisakh to Ashar, 1391 B.S. But he refused to accept the same. The defendants thereupon sent the rent for the aforesaid months to the plaintiff on 7.7.84 through rent money order which was refused on 10.7.84 and the defendants received back the same on 14.7.84 and the defendants have been depositing the rent since then in the House Rent Control Case No. 38 of 1984 and as such they are not defaulters. The defendants further case is that they paid rent to the Government and taxes to the Pourashava for the suit premises amounting to more than Tk.500/-. The plaintiff demanded illegal money for the premises from the defendants which they did not agree and for that the plaintiff filed the suit for same illegal gains and to earn a handsome amount by letting out the premises to 3rd party. 

 4. By the impugned judgment and decree the learned Small Cause Court Judge dismissed the suit on the findings that the four rent receipts Exts. Ka-Ka(3) and the six counter foils of rent receipts up to 30th Aswin, 1387 Exts 1-1(e) B.S. show that the plaintiff accepted the rent from the defendants in lump for few month at a time, that the plaintiff failed to prove that there was written agreement for payment of rent due for a month within the expiry of the months for which it was due and that it appeared from the rent receipts produced in Court that there was an oral agreement between the former Mutwalli and the defendants for payment of rent in yearly instalment and in such circumstances when the defendants paid rent in yearly instalment they could not be called defaulters. 

 6. Mr. Subodh Ranjan Dutta, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has submitted that in the absence of any written contract between the plaintiff-landlord and the tenant-defendants the rent was payable within the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent was payable under the provision of section 18(5) of the Premise Rent Control Ordinance, 1986 and as such the learned Small Cause Court Judge committed an error of law in holding that the rent was payable in yearly instalment. 

 7. Mr. Dutta has further submitted that the acceptance of rent by the plaintiff by instalment or in a lump will not disentitle the plaintiff to get a decree for ejectment if the defendants are found to be defaulters. 

 9. The last submission of Mr. Dutta is that the learned Small Cause Court Judge failed to consider that the transmission cost was not deposited along with the monthly rent in House Rent Control Case No. 38 of 1984 and the deposit having not been made as per provisions of section 19(1) (b) read with section 18(5) of the Ordinance the said deposit would not be considered as valid deposit. In support of his submission be has relied upon the case of Mir M.A. Razzaque and others Vs. Md. Abdul Hai Patwari 5 B.L.D (AD) 97. 

 10. In reply to the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, has submitted by making reference to the case of Md. Golam Hossain Vs. Mst. Asia Khaiun Chowdhury, 40 DLR (AD) 1 that in view of the pleadings and evidence on record the present case is an example of waiver and acquiescence and as such although the defendants made payment of rent in a lump in yearly instalment they cannot he called defaulters and in this connection Mr. Quayum has pointed out that in paragraph 2 of the plaint the plaintiff stated that whenever the plaintiff demanded rent from the defendants they deferred payment on various pretexts and ultimately they would pay rent for 2/3 months at a time and the plaintiff would accept the rent out of kindness, that the defendants pleaded waiver and ac-quiescence in paragraph 6 of the written statement, that the petitioner as P.W. 1 stated that the defendants entered the suit premises in 1380 B.S. on same terms with the former Mutwalli Rahmatullah and accordingly the former Mutwalli used to receive rent in lump by instalment and the plaintiff signed the rent receipt Ext. A series dated 1.7.87 B.S. for the months from Chaitra to Aswin, 1387 B.S. 

 11. In reply Mr. Dutta has submitted that the statement in the plaint that the defendants would not pay rent in spite of demand and that they paid rent for 2/3 months at a time and the plaintiff accepted the same out of kindness does not amount to waiver as contended on behalf of the defendants. He has referred to the statement of D.W.1 (defendant No. 3) to the effect that when the present Mutwalli was appointed the defendants had an understanding with him with regard to the mode of payment of rent. 

 12. Mr. Quayum has further submitted that the payment of municipal taxes by the defendants in addition to their payment of rent shows that they were not defaulters. 

 To this Mr. Dutta has submitted that payment of municipal taxes in excess of payment of rent does not and cannot show that the defendants are not defaulters. 

 13. Mr. Quayum has next submitted that the plaintiff sought to evict the defendants only for getting salami from new tenants which is not allowed under section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1986. In elaboration of his submission he has pointed out the statement of plaintiff P.W. 1 to the affect that there is provision for letting out the premises on receipt of salami and that the salami of the suit premises would be Tk. 20,000/-, 25,000/-. 

 "From the evidence it appears that the defendant-appellants have on various occasions paid rents for several months at a time. There is no controversy regarding such lump sum payments of rent. What is, however, important to notice about such payments is that while granting receipts for them the plaintiff respondent took care in giving such receipts month wise. A question is do the facts constitute an evidence of a contract between the parties waiving the right to receive rent within the 15th day following that month for which rent has become due. Secondly even if it does whether sub-section (5) of section 18 of the Ordinance contemplates this kind of contract or an oral agreement. On referring to the precise provisions of this sub-section it is seen that the expression used therein are within the time fixed in the contract or by the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable." The portion under-lined by me refer to the existence of the contract between the landlord and the tenant. From the use of the preposition "in" before the expressions "the contract", the intention of the legislature seems to be clear. There might have been some scope for controversy if the preposition 'by' was used instead of the preposition 'in'. As it is, the contract referred to here in this sub-section means a written contract, and not an oral contract. The Ordinance lays down the deadline for rents to be paid by a tenant, that is, by the 15th day of the month next following that for a which the rent is payable'. If this time limit has to be varied by a landlord and his tenant, it obviously implies something in writing, which is not the case here. Moreover, defendant-appellants tried to establish the so-called con-tract by referring to the practice of the parties of payment of rent in lump sum amount and the acceptance of the same by the landlord at a time. It has been pointed out by the respondent's Counsel that though there has been lump sum payments and receipts, the plaintiff-respondent never accepted such lump sum amounts by granting one receipt. Receipts issued by the Plaintiff-respondent show that they were issued month-wise, that is, one receipt for one month and the date of granting receipt was put within the month before the 15th day of the following month. The learned counsel further submitted that the regular payment of lump sum rents for several months at a time and the receipts thereof granted in the aforesaid manner did not create any express or implied contract varying the deadline of payment of rents by a monthly tenant as provided in the Ordinance, nor did such conduct constitute a waiver of the respondent landlord's right to receive rents by the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable. In the absence of any contract and also on the failure of the defendant-appellants to prove the extistence of an oral contract between the parties to the effect that the respondent would collect rents for several months at a time according to his convenience the defendant-appellant must be held to be defaulters within the meaning of the terms used in sub-section(5) of section 18 of the Ordinance." 

 "under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance a tenant is under an obligation to pay rent within certain period after the same has become due. Section 18 provides that in the absence of any contract to the contrary between the landlord and tenant to pay the monthly rent within a certain date it must be paid within the 15th day of the next month. These statutory restrictions relating to payment of monthly rent within certain date, if disregarded by the tenant, disentitles him to the protection against eviction for default in payment of rent. By judicial interpretation of these provisions which impose such restrictions the only exception which, if established, can take the tenant out of the mischief of those restrictions, is waiver, that is, if the tenant succeeds in showing that though he defaulted in paying rent within the due date or dates, the landlord accepted the rent without any objection or protest. Mere acceptance of rent is not sufficient to constitute waiver. Whether there has been any waiver by the landlord must be gathered from the facts of the case. Vide Ramzan Ali Mistry Vs. Hedayetullah (1979) 31 DLR (AD) 183: 

 "There may be a case of waiver or acceptance or such supervening facts and circumstances as to make the compliance with the enactment beyond the control of the tenant. However, it will depend on the facts of a particular case to see whether there has been default in the payment of rent in terms of the statute but once the fact is established in terms of the Ordinance, legal consequence following therefrom cannot be averted. 

 "Once a default occurs subsequent acceptance of the rent in lump by the landlord, docs not, in the absence of any positive proof of his intention to waive such default, amount to waiver so as to entitle him to the protection against the consequence of default, that is, eviction." 

 Thus even on the ratio of the case of M.A. Haque (40 DLR (AD) 109) and the majority view of Binning & Co. Ltd. (40 DLR AD 89) there is no escape from arriving at a conclusion that the defendant had made out a case of waiver and acquiescence in the facts and circumstance of the case at the earliest opportunity. Evidence that has been led shows that this was the arrangement between the landlord and the tenant that the Karmachari would come and collect the rent. This practice continued for 16 years. In the meantime the original lessor died and his son for some time managed the property and ultimately it devolved upon the plaintiff. It is the plaintiffs son who is now looking after the property. The trial Court noticed that the management of the property had been well established by the rent receipts Exts A(1) to A(61) which were issued in lump and it was not granted in month wise receipt as was the case in the earlier decision e.g. M/s. M.A. Hoque. 

 20. In the instant case the plea of waiver was not raised or agitated at the trial and no such issue was framed there. In the Appellate Division Case in a 40 DLR (AD) 89 it has been held that the tenant is required to take the plea of waiver in the pleading and at the trial where it should be raised as an issue. In the plaint the plaintiff asserted that whenever he demanded rent from the defendants they deferred payment of rent on various pretexts and ultimately they would pay rent for 2/3 months at a time and the plaintiff would receive the rent out of kindness. 

 22. In the instant case apparently the facts are different from those of the case in 40 DLR (AD) 1 inasmuch as in the said case that evidence showed that there was an arrangement between the landlord and tenant that the Karmachari would come and collect the rent and this practice continued for 16 years and that it was noticed by the trial court that the management of the property had been established by rent receipts Ext. A(1)-A(61) which were issued in lump and not granted month-wise. But in the instant case there was no arrangement between the plaintiff and the defendants for collection of rents by Karmacharies in lump for few months and no such practice continued for a long time. Again, there is no admission by the plaintiff in the instant case that he had no grievance as to mode of payment of rent in lump and the instant case is not a case of waiver and acquiescence. In these circumstances, the case in 40 DLR (AD) 1 has no application in the instant case. 

 23. As already noted it has been held in 40 DLR ( AD) 109 that in the absence of any contract if the rent is not paid within 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable as per section 18(5) of the Ordinance the tenant will become a defaulter. It has been further held in the said case that the word 'contract' means written contract. In the instant case there is no written contract between the landlord and the tenants and as such the tenant defendents are liable to pay the rent by the 15th day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable. 

 24. In 40 DLR (AD) 89 the Appellate Division has held that the payment of rent in lump does not save a tenant from making him defaulter and once a default occurs subsequent acceptance of rent in lump by the landlord can not protect the tenant from being a defaulter in the absence of any positive proof of his intention to waive such default and as already noticed there is no positive proof of the intention of the plaintiff to waive the default in the instant case. 

 25. The payment of municipal taxes by the defendants in excess of payment of rent, I think, can not save the defendants from being defaulter if they are otherwise found to be defaulters. 

 26. The statement of the plaintiff as P.W. 1 as referred to above docs not show that he sought to evict the defendants only for getting salami from the new tenants but the plaintiff sought to evict the defend ants because they did not pay rents regularly. That being so section 10 of the Ordinance is not attracted. 

 27. The information slip Annexure A showing that the transmission cost was not deposited in the Rent Control Case, I think, can not be looked into at this stage because it not being a public document the matter should have been raised before the trial Court and considered there on evidence and for that the case in BLD (AD) 94 need not be considered. 

 28. In the above circumstances, it is found in the light of decisions in 40 DLR (AD) 109 and 89 that the defendants are defaulters and the learned Small Cause Court Judge is not correct in holding the view that the defendants are not so merely because of the fact that the plaintiff accepted payments of rent from them in lump for few months by instalment. The judgment and decree of the learned Small Cause Court Judge are therefore liable to be interfered with.
